title: Review: Density; Upthrust / Archimedes' principle; Viscosity and Stokes' law; Springs and Hooke's law; Stress, strain and Young modulus
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: D06-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; FL05-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; FL05-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; FL03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: D06-1#N.12, FL01-1#N.4, FL03-1#N.7, FL05-1#N.2, MT01-1#N.6, D06-1#N.2b, FL05-1#N.10, MT01-1#N.9, FL05-1#N.5b, FL05-1#N.7. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Extension
items.clue: Stretched length minus the original length, not the whole length.

items.label: Viscosity
items.clue: Internal friction between layers of a fluid, symbol η, measured in Pa s.

items.label: Turbulent flow
items.clue: Swirling eddies caused by faster or larger objects, making drag much larger.

items.label: Archimedes' principle
items.clue: Statement that the upward push from a fluid equals the weight of fluid displaced.

questions.stem: A spring that obeys Hooke's law is 15.0 cm long when it supports a 3.0 N load and 18.0 cm long when it supports a 6.0 N load. What is its natural (unloaded) length?
questions.explanation: The extra 3.0 N adds 3.0 cm, so the extension is 1.0 cm per newton. With 3.0 N on, the extension is 3.0 cm: natural length = 15.0 − 3.0 = 12.0 cm.

questions.stem: The density of aluminium is 2.7 g cm⁻³. What is the volume, in m³, of an aluminium block of mass 0.081 kg?

A foam ball of volume V would float, but it is held at rest completely under water by a light string tied to the bottom of a tank. The density of the foam is a quarter of the density ρ of water. Which expression gives the tension in the string?

Sphere X moves through an oil at speed v and feels a viscous drag F. Sphere Y, with twice the radius of X, moves through the same oil at half the speed. Stokes' law applies. What is the viscous drag on Y?
questions.explanation: F = 6πηrv. Doubling r doubles the drag; halving v halves it. Overall: unchanged.

questions.stem: A student repeats the Young modulus experiment with the same loads on a wire of the same metal and diameter, but only one tenth as long. The extension is read with the same scale. What is the main effect?

options.text: Each extension is ten times smaller, so its percentage uncertainty is ten times larger.
The Young modulus found is ten times smaller.
The stress is ten times larger, so the wire passes its limit of proportionality.
Nothing changes, as the Young modulus is a property of the material.

questions.explanation: Strain is unchanged, so extension ∝ original length. The same reading error is now ten times larger as a fraction of the extension.

questions.stem: In a lab, a student models a spring as a light spring that obeys Hooke's law. Which statement describes how the spring's force behaves in this model?

options.text: Its force is proportional to its length, measured end to end.
Its force doubles when its extension doubles.
Its force is the same however far it is stretched or compressed.
Its force depends on how fast the attached object is moving.

questions.stem: Two water droplets in fog fall at terminal velocity through still air. Droplet P has twice the radius of droplet Q. Stokes' law applies to both. What is the terminal velocity of P divided by the terminal velocity of Q?
questions.explanation: Weight ∝ r³ (the air's upward push on a droplet is negligible); drag ∝ rv. Balancing: r³ ∝ rv, so v ∝ r². Doubling r gives 2² = 4 times the terminal velocity.

questions.stem: Two cables are made of the same aluminium alloy and carry the same load. Cable Q is 3 times as long as cable P and has 3 times its diameter. Both obey Hooke's law. What is the extension of Q divided by the extension of P?
questions.explanation: Extension = force × length ÷ (area × Young modulus). Same force and material; length × 3; area × 3² = 9. Ratio = 3/9 = 1/3.

questions.stem: A small aluminium sphere of radius 0.50 mm falls at terminal velocity through glycerol. The density of aluminium is 2.7 × 10³ kg m⁻³. The density of glycerol is 1.26 × 10³ kg m⁻³ and its viscosity is 1.4 Pa s. Take g = 9.81 m s⁻². What is the terminal velocity of the sphere?

A student measures the viscosity of an oil by the falling-ball method on a warm day, with the oil at 28 °C. Her value is lower than the data-book value, which is quoted for 20 °C. Which is the most likely explanation?

options.text: She started timing before the ball had reached terminal velocity.
The oil was warmer than 20 °C, and a liquid's viscosity falls as it warms.
She used the ball's diameter in place of its radius in her calculation.
She left the upthrust on the ball out of her calculation.

questions.explanation: Warmer oil is less viscous, so the ball falls faster and her η is lower. Her value may well be right for 28 °C: a viscosity needs its temperature.
